‘Never!’ the girl answered.

‘Tell me why.’

‘For one reason,’ she replied resolutely, ‘one reason the lady knows, and will support me in—I am sure she will, because she has promised. And for another reason as well: wicked as his life has been, mine has been wicked too. Many of us have followed the same ways together, and I won't betray people who might—any one of them—have betrayed me, but never did, bad though they are.’

‘Then,’ said the gentleman promptly, as though this were the point he had wished to reach, ‘place Monks in my hands, and let me deal with him.’

‘And suppose he betrays the others?’

‘I give you my word that, if the truth is wrung from him, the business shall end there. There must be things in Oliver's short history which it would be painful to expose to public view; and once we have learned the truth, the others shall escape untouched.’

‘And suppose you don't?’ the girl asked.

‘Then,’ the gentleman continued, ‘this Fagin shall not be brought before the law without your agreement. In that event, I believe I could give you reasons that would persuade you to grant it.’

‘Does the lady promise that?’ asked the girl.

‘I do,’ Rose answered. ‘You have my sincere and faithful word.’

‘Monks would never discover where your information came from?’ said the girl, after a brief silence.

‘Never,’ replied the gentleman. ‘We would use the information against him in such a manner that he could not even guess.’

‘I have lied, and lived among liars, since I was a little child,’ said the girl after another pause, ‘but I will believe your words.’

When both had assured her that she could safely trust them, she began, in a voice so low that the listener often struggled even to catch the meaning, to give the name and position of the public-house from which she had been followed that night. Her occasional pauses suggested that the gentleman was taking hurried notes of what she told him. Having fully described the surrounding streets, the best place from which to watch the house unnoticed, and the night and hour at which Monks most commonly visited it, she appeared to reflect for a few moments, trying to summon a clearer recollection of his features and appearance.

‘He is tall,’ the girl said, ‘and powerfully built, though not stout. He walks in a skulking fashion, and keeps glancing over his shoulder as he goes, first to one side and then the other.’

As my father's surname was Pirrip and my Christian name Philip, my baby tongue could turn the two into nothing longer or clearer than Pip. Thus I named myself Pip, and Pip I came to be called.

For my father's family name, Pirrip, I rely upon his gravestone and my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. Having never seen either parent, nor any portrait of them—their time was well before photographs—I drew my earliest, unreasonable notions of their appearance from their tombstones. The form of the lettering on my father's suggested to me, oddly enough, a square, stout, dark man with black curls. The style and flourish of the words ‘Also Georgiana Wife of the Above’ led me to conclude, in my childish way, that my mother had freckles and poor health. Five little lozenge-shaped stones, each some eighteen inches long, stood neatly in a row beside their grave, commemorating five small brothers who had abandoned the attempt to earn a living exceedingly early in that universal contest. To these stones I owed my firmly held belief that all five had arrived in the world lying on their backs, hands in their trouser pockets, and had never withdrawn them during their earthly existence.

We lived in the marsh country beside the river, within twenty miles of the sea if one followed its windings. My earliest vivid, comprehensive sense of what things were seems to have come on one memorable, bitter afternoon as evening approached. Then I understood with certainty that this desolate, nettle-covered place was the churchyard; that Philip Pirrip, formerly of this parish, and also Georgiana, wife of the above, lay dead and buried; that Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger, infant sons of those aforesaid, lay dead and buried too; that the flat, dark waste beyond the churchyard, crossed by dikes, banks, and gates and dotted with grazing cattle, was the marshes; that the low, lead-coloured streak beyond it was the river; that the distant wild den sending forth the wind was the sea; and that the little shivering bundle, frightened by everything and beginning to weep, was Pip.

‘Stop that noise!’ shouted a dreadful voice, as a man sprang up among the graves beside the church porch. ‘Be quiet, you little devil, or I'll slit your throat!’

A terrifying man, dressed entirely in rough grey cloth, with a heavy iron fastened to his leg.

Sir Walter had rented an excellent house in Camden Place, an elevated and imposing situation appropriate to a gentleman of consequence; he and Elizabeth were established there to their great contentment.

Anne crossed its threshold with a heavy heart, foreseeing months of confinement and anxiously asking herself, ‘Oh, when shall I get away from you again?’ Yet the unexpected warmth of her reception afforded her some comfort. Her father and sister were pleased to see her, eager to display the house and furnishings, and greeted her kindly. At dinner, the advantage of having her complete a party of four was remarked upon.

Mrs. Clay was exceedingly agreeable and full of smiles, but her politeness and smiling were more to be expected. Anne had always known she would assume the proper manner on her arrival; the graciousness of the others came as a surprise. Clearly they were in the best of spirits, and she was soon to hear why. They had little desire to hear her news. After fishing for compliments about how sorely their former neighbours missed them, which Anne could not supply, they offered only a few indifferent questions before claiming the conversation entirely for themselves. Uppercross interested them not at all, Kellynch hardly more: Bath was everything.

They delighted in telling her that Bath had surpassed their expectations in every particular. Their house was unquestionably the finest in Camden Place. Their drawing-rooms enjoyed numerous distinct advantages over every other drawing-room they had seen or heard described, and were equally superior in decoration and the taste displayed in their furniture. Their acquaintance was much coveted. Everyone wished to call upon them. They had declined many introductions, yet cards were continually being left by people whose names meant nothing to them.

Here was an ample store of pleasure. Could Anne wonder at her father and sister's happiness? She could hardly wonder, yet she could only sigh that her father felt no loss of standing in his altered circumstances, missed none of the responsibilities and dignity of a landowner living on his estate, and found so much to gratify his vanity in a town's small affairs. And she had to sigh, smile, and wonder together as Elizabeth opened the folding doors and passed triumphantly between the two drawing-rooms, boasting of their size. How could a woman who had presided over Kellynch Hall discover spaciousness worth boasting of between walls perhaps thirty feet apart?

Nor was this the whole of their happiness. They had Mr. Elliot as well.
